c0676: An LLC separates personal and business liability, which matters when you serve hot drinks and run a generator at other people's events. An S corp election can cut self-employment tax once profit is steady; ask your accountant when it pays off.
c0692: Apply on your state tax agency website. Hosted bookings are usually taxed as catering, and in many states that means the whole invoice: coffee, baristas and extras, and in some states travel. At festivals and farmers markets you collect tax drink by drink, and you may need to register where you sell. Check your state's rule before you quote.
c0700: Bring the Word plan, the Excel projections and written quotes for the cart, the espresso machines, the grinders and the trailer. SBA 7(a) loans go through participating banks: ask what owner equity they expect and how long approval takes, and do not buy the cart before the plan review and the loan are approved.
c0701: Have an attorney review your coffee catering service agreement, starting from the kit's template
c0704: Start from the contract in this kit. Ask for a retainer of 30-50% to hold the date and credit it toward the price, the balance due 14 days before and the final guest count 10 days before. Add cancellation tiers with no gaps, service hours and the price of an extra hour, the outlet (110V or 220V, within a set number of feet) or a generator fee, a travel fee beyond your free radius, alt milks, a rain plan and the certificate of insurance for the venue. Reuse it for every event.
c0705: Write your HACCP-based food safety plan for the cart, with a written cold holding procedure for milk
c0708: Milk is a TCS food: keep it at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (the FDA Food Code cold-holding limit) in the refrigerator and in the coolers, and date every opened container. Use potable water from an approved source in food-grade tanks, wash your hands first, and wipe and purge the steam wand and clean the pitchers between drinks. Flag the allergens: milk, soy and tree nuts, plus wheat and egg in pastries. Buy pastries only from a licensed bakery.
c0718: Choose a permitted commissary: water fill and gray water dump, milk refrigeration, dry storage and a place for the cart and the trailer
c0721: Visit at least three and ask first: can you fill potable water and dump gray water here, is there cold storage for milk, and where do the cart and the trailer stay? Compare hours, storage and the deposit. Do you need a commissary for a coffee cart? Usually yes, though some counties exempt self-contained units, so ask yours in writing (California's rule is Health & Safety Code §114295; Washington has an exemption under RCW 43.20.148, as examples). Never prep or store from home.
c0725: Your health department asks for it with the permit application. It should name your hours, water fill and gray water dump, storage for the cart and the trailer, and cleaning duties. Keep a signed copy on file, and a commissary log on board where your county asks for one (Washington does).
c0726: Apply for the mobile food unit permit and get the plan review BEFORE you buy the cart
c0729: Ask the county for its plan review checklist: NSF certifications, tank sizes, handwashing sink, refrigerator and an electrical plan. As an example, Snohomish County, WA charges $1,100 for the plan review and $500-1,025 for the annual permit, and wants electrical approval first. Ask whether a cart at private catered events counts as a mobile food unit or as a caterer in your county.
c0733: Your mobile food unit permit does not always cover a festival. Each public or community event may need its own temporary food permit; ask the county health department and the organizer how far ahead to apply.
c0734: Check with your fire marshal about the generator
c0737: Without grease vapors you do not need a hood, but a generator does have rules. As one example, a city fire department checklist (Lenexa, Kansas, based on NFPA 96) asks for a free-standing generator at least 12 ft (3.7 m) from the unit and 10 ft (3 m) from buildings, with an extinguisher on hand, and some states, such as New Jersey, may require a fire safety permit where a generator is used. Rules differ by city and fire district: confirm with your fire marshal.
c0738: Buy your espresso cart with the plan review checklist in hand
c0741: Make sure it matches what your county approves: NSF certification, a handwashing sink, potable and gray water tanks of the size your county asks for, and an under-counter refrigerator. If you buy a used cart, have an equipment technician inspect it and check for liens.
c0742: Title and register the trailer, and buy commercial auto and equipment-in-transit coverage
c0745: Register the trailer at your state DMV in the business name. Commercial auto must cover the tow and the trailer; inland marine covers the cart, the machines and the grinders in transit. Check your vehicle's towing capacity and the hitch rating.
c0746: Buy and fit out the enclosed trailer: ramp, E-track anchors, wheel chocks for the cart, shelving and wrap
c0749: Fit E-track anchors and wheel chocks so the cart and the portable bar travel strapped down, add shelving and non-slip liners so loads cannot shift, and put on your logo wrap. Check that your insurer covers the fit-out.
c0753: Ask in writing for a general liability or BOP policy of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate with unlimited additional insureds. Venues and planners ask for a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as additional insured; ask your broker for same-day COIs.
c0754: Set your alcohol policy: no espresso martinis or liquor in your drinks without a license
c0757: You cannot sell alcohol without a liquor license, so refer espresso martini requests to a licensed mobile bar (see the Mobile Bar Business Plan Kit). Ask your broker how your general liability policy treats alcohol you do not sell, so there are no surprises if a host brings their own.
c0761: Required in almost every state once you have employees, including part-time event baristas (Texas is the exception: optional there, but venues and lenders often ask for it). Premiums depend on payroll and class code.
c0762: Set up your waste plan: gray water, coffee grounds and milk containers
c0765: Dump gray water only at the commissary, never in a venue's sink or a storm drain. Send coffee grounds to compost where your commissary or city offers it, and recycle milk containers. Ask the commissary what it already handles.
c0775: A full-service espresso bar, a self-serve coffee station with drop-off cold brew and a guest-pay pop-up need different equipment. Rent what you use rarely and buy what you use at nearly every event.
c0776: Buy under-counter refrigerators, coolers with ice packs, calibrated thermometers and airpots
c0779: Keep milk at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (the FDA Food Code cold-holding limit) with an under-counter refrigerator at each station and coolers with ice packs for the reserve. Calibrate thermometers in ice water and keep spares in the trailer. Airpots keep batch brew hot through the service window.
c0780: Open wholesale accounts with a specialty roaster, a milk distributor and a compostable cup supplier
c0783: Buy coffee by the lb from a specialty roaster (roasted 1-3 weeks before the event) and milk and oat milk from a distributor or a cash-and-carry. Compare delivery minimums and price lists, and order compostable cups where your city requires them.
c0784: Buy the espresso machines (a 2-group at 220V plus a compact 2-group) and the grinders, then install and dial them in
c0787: Confirm the amps and the plug before your first event: the 220V machine needs a dedicated NEMA 6-20 circuit (15-17 A) and the compact one pulls about 14 A. Install both, dial in the grinders at 18 g (0.63 oz) in and 36 g (1.27 oz) out, and pull test shots. A room without a 220V circuit needs a generator.
c0788: Stock smallwares: milk pitchers, scales, tampers, knock boxes, shot glasses, towels and sanitizer
c0791: Buy pitchers in several sizes so you can steam 8 oz (240 ml) or 12 oz (355 ml) drinks without waste, plus scales, tampers, knock boxes, shot glasses, towels, sanitizer buckets and test strips. Standardize sizes so everything stacks and fits the trailer.
c0792: Set up your syrups, sauces, alt milks and tea: recipes, labels and an allergen list per drink
c0795: Write a recipe and a label for each house-made syrup, and decide which milks you carry (oat, almond, soy) and whether you serve chai. Keep an allergen list per drink: milk, soy and tree nuts, and oat is gluten-free only if labeled gluten-free. Plan milk in oz per drink (8 oz, or 240 ml) and in gallons per event.
c0796: Build the second station: portable espresso bar, menu and signage, cup display and condiment station
c0799: The second station takes the overflow at big events and covers indoor rooms. Set up the portable bar with a short menu and signage, a cup display and a condiment station. Bring cords and a power strip with GFCI, and the generator for outdoor events.
c0800: Plan your espresso water: food-grade tanks, pump and a filter or softener
c0803: Water quality decides how your drinks taste and how long your machines last. Use food-grade tanks and a pump, and add a filter or a softener depending on how hard your water is. Ask your county for the minimum tank volume, and plan the fill and dump routine at the commissary.
c0804: Choose compostable cups, lids, sleeves and napkins for your drinks
c0807: Buy compostable cups in 8, 12 and 16 oz (240, 355 and 475 ml) with lids, sleeves, wooden stirrers, napkins and cold cups. Use compostable items where your city requires them (Seattle, as an example), and skip foam. Test that the lids seal before you buy a case.
c0808: Log milk temperature at every station
c0811: Check the refrigerator thermometer at each station and write down the temperature when you load, when you set up and mid-service. Milk must stay at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (the FDA Food Code cold-holding limit). Keep the logs after every event.
c0816: Run a full test event with both stations at full speed
c0819: Simulate a line of guests with both stations running. Count drinks per hour per barista and how much coffee, milk and how many cups you use, then use those numbers to calibrate the kit calculator.
c0822: Set a barista plan per event
c0825: One barista makes about 50-65 drinks an hour, so 2 baristas on 2 machines handle about 100, and 2-3 baristas cover around 250 guests (Flashquotes). Write the ratio down and use it to price labor in every quote.
c0829: Event baristas are usually employees, not contractors (FLSA economic reality test; California AB5). Misclassification brings back wages and penalties, so pay them hourly on W-2 payroll, never 1099.
c0845: A mandatory service charge is not a tip: the part paid out to staff is wages (IRS Rev. Rul. 2012-18). A gratuity is voluntary and goes to staff. Keep them on separate invoice lines and check your state's sales tax rule. Use a tip jar only if the host accepts it, and the tips belong to the team.
c0850: Train baristas on safety: steam and hot water burns, refueling the generator, cords and GFCI power strips
c0853: Teach everyone to avoid steam and hot water burns, to refuel the generator only when it is cold and away from guests, to tape down cords and trip hazards, and to plug into GFCI power strips. Name who watches the equipment at all times during service.
c0854: Cover OSHA basics: burns, lifting the cart and machines, towing the trailer and wet floors
c0857: Train staff to lift the cart and the machines with two people and up the ramp, to hitch and tow the trailer safely, and to watch for wet floors. Keep an injury log and a first-aid kit in the trailer and at every event.
c0858: Train your service protocol: menu, standards, latte art, greeting, line handling and allergens
c0861: Run a pre-event briefing every time. Set your standards: a double shot at 18 g (0.63 oz) in and about 36 g (1.27 oz) out, 8 oz (240 ml) milk drinks, latte art, a greeting and how to move the line. Label milk, soy and tree nuts, and wheat and egg in pastries; oat milk is gluten-free only if labeled gluten-free.
c0864: Create your brand, logo, a short menu and photos of the cart at real events
c0867: Keep the menu short: espresso classics, signature and seasonal drinks, cold brew, chai and hot chocolate, with oat milk included. Photograph the cart at real events and the latte art; photos sell catering far better than menus.
c0880: Join GigSalad, Thumbtack and The Bash for private parties
c0883: These marketplaces charge a commission or a cost per lead. Build it into your prices from the start and track your cost per booking.
c0891: Build your quote in the kit calculator: cost per drink, price per guest and per service hour, baristas and power. Log every inquiry in your CRM and follow up within 48 hours. Pick software that sends the quote, collects the e-signature and takes the retainer by card or ACH.
c0895: Make a list of nearby offices, coworking spaces and event planners and offer a free hour of espresso at an open house. Corporate events are about 69.3% of coffee cart bookings on Flashquotes and they fill your weekdays, so follow up every contact.
c0896: Post latte art and the cart at events on Instagram and social media
c0899: Share photos and short videos with the client's permission. Use text messages for quick follow-ups, and keep every inquiry in your CRM.
c0911: Host an open house with a coffee bar for planners, venue managers and corporate event buyers. Ask your local wedding venues when the next bridal show is and reserve a booth early.
c0917: Confirm the guest count, service hours, menu and milks, allergies, power and who your contact is on the day. Send the summary in writing, and remember the final guest count is due 10 days before.
c0918: Check the venue 2 weeks out: outlet, floor, access, trailer parking and rules
c0921: Confirm the outlet (110V or 220V), its amps and how far it is from your station, a level floor, indoor or outdoor, access and an elevator for the cart, and where the trailer will park. A 220V machine needs a dedicated circuit, so settle it in writing. Ask the venue for its rules in writing, and photograph the space.
c0926: Order coffee, milk and cups with a buffer, and prep cold brew and syrups the day before
c0928: 1 week out, then the day before
c0929: Order coffee (roasted 1-3 weeks earlier) and milks with a small buffer, plus cups. Brew the cold brew (12-24 hours) and make the syrups at the commissary the day before, labeled and chilled, and build one production list with who does what.
c0930: Load the trailer from the checklist: cart and bar strapped down, machines, grinders, cords, generator and milk in coolers
c0933: Check the cart and the portable bar are strapped down, then the machines, grinders, cords and generator, the milk in coolers at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, the water tanks filled at the commissary and the cups against the list. Write down the milk temperature when you load and again when you arrive.
c0934: Arrive 1-1.5 hours early and set up: handwashing first, then warm up the machines and dial in the grinders
c0937: Set up the handwashing station first, then the cart and the portable bar; setup takes about 1 hour. Warm up the machines, dial in the grinders and pull test shots, then serve during the booked service window. Count the drinks you serve: the number feeds your weekly review.
c0938: Break down: backflush and clean the machines, steam wands and grinders
c0941: Backflush the machines, clean the steam wands and the grinders, and dump gray water only at the commissary. Throw away opened milk that spent time above 41 °F (5 °C). At festivals and farmers markets, reconcile your sales with the organizer before you leave.
c0946: Review every week: drinks per guest, drinks per hour per barista, coffee and milk used, cost per drink and hours per event
c0949: Compare drinks per guest, drinks per hour per barista, coffee and milk used, cost per drink and staff hours with what the calculator projected. Small gaps add up quickly across a season.
